checklist: Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Create a new level named L_Terrain_01. Open Landscape Mode, go to the Manage tab and choose New. Keep the landscape small: the default size or less is plenty.
Select the Sculpt tool and raise one hill. Then hold Shift while you sculpt to dig one hollow, because Shift makes the tool push the ground down.
Use the Smooth tool over the edges until nothing looks like a spike.
Use the Ramp tool to make one path from the low ground to the top of the hill. The Ramp tool builds a straight, even slope between two points that you place.
Place a Player Start in the level and set the GameMode to the Third Person GameMode. Then walk the path in PIE, which means Play In Editor.
Find every place where the character slides back or gets stuck. Smooth or flatten the ground there.
Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Open Project Settings and go to the Rendering section. Confirm that Dynamic Global Illumination Method is set to Lumen.

Open a room level of your own, or build a simple room in a new level from cubes: a floor, four walls and a ceiling, with one wall in a strong color. In the room, place one Point Light, one Spot Light and one Rect Light. Set the Mobility of all three to Movable, which means the light is fully dynamic and can change while the game runs.
Change the Intensity, the Attenuation Radius (how far the light reaches) and the color of each light. For the Spot Light, also change the cone angles.
Aim the Rect Light at the colored wall. Watch how Lumen bounces the color of the wall onto the floor.
Change the Mobility of one light to Static, and note what the tooltip or the warning says.

EAQ10.brief: Exposure is how bright the camera makes the picture. By default Unreal uses auto exposure, which slowly changes the brightness like your eyes do when you enter a dark room. This hides lighting problems and makes every screenshot look different. In this quest you lock the exposure to one fixed value with a Post Process Volume, so that you see the real brightness of a room.
checklist: Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open a room level of your own, or build a simple room in a new Basic level from cubes: a floor, four walls, a ceiling and one doorway that lets the daylight in. Add a Post Process Volume and tick Infinite Extent (Unbound). This makes the volume apply everywhere, no matter where the camera is.
Start PIE and walk from the bright doorway into a dark corner. Watch how auto exposure slowly changes the brightness.
In the Exposure section of the volume, set Metering Mode to Manual. Then adjust Exposure Compensation until you can see the room clearly.
Walk the same path again. The brightness should now stay the same.
Save a camera bookmark, and take a screenshot from it before the lock and after the lock.

EAQ11.brief: Foliage means plants, rocks and other small meshes that you paint onto the ground in large numbers with Foliage Mode. Foliage makes a space feel real, but it must not stand in the way of the player. In this quest you paint two foliage types along a path and make sure that nothing blocks the route.
checklist: Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Open a level of your own that has a Landscape with a path on it. If you have none, create a new level, open Landscape Mode, choose New on the Manage tab, and sculpt one hill with a path up to it. Open Foliage Mode and add two foliage types: one bush, and one small grass mesh or rock mesh. The Starter Content has a bush and a rock in its Props folder.
Paint both types along the edges of the path. Hold Shift and paint to erase anything that lands on the path.
Open the bush foliage type and lower its Density. Stop when you can still see clearly where the edges of the path are.
Set the Collision Preset of the grass type to NoCollision, so that the player walks through it.
Walk the path in PIE. Nothing on the path should stop you or catch you.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open BP_ThirdPersonCharacter and select the Capsule Component, the invisible shape that collides with the world. Write down its Capsule Radius and Capsule Half Height.
Select the Character Movement component. Write down Max Step Height, Walkable Floor Angle, Jump Z Velocity and Gravity Scale.
Create a new level named L_MetricsGym. Build a row of steps (15, 30, 45 and 60 cm high), a row of ledges (from 100 to 250 cm, 25 cm apart) and a row of gaps (from 100 to 500 cm, 50 cm apart).
Build three doorways. Make the first as wide as the capsule diameter, the second as wide as the diameter + 40 cm, and the third a width that feels comfortable to you.
Start PIE and test every piece. Note the highest step you can walk up, the highest ledge you can jump onto, and the widest gap you can jump over.
Put a Text Render actor next to each piece as a label, so that the numbers are visible in screenshots.
Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Create a new level named L_Toolkit. You will build the same small room three times, with a floor, walls and one doorway.
Build version A from cubes that you take from the Place Actors panel and scale to the right size.
Build version B with geometry brushes. Use one additive box for the room, and one subtractive box that cuts out the doorway.
Build version C with the CubeGrid tool in Modeling Mode. Set the grid to a size that fits a character, such as 50 or 100 cm.
Change the width of the doorway in all three versions. Time how long each change takes.
Write down which tool you would use for a quick room, which for a big irregular shape, and which for a piece you want to use again.
Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Create a new level named L_Routes_01. Place a start and a goal about 40 to 60 m apart. A lit box is fine as the goal.
Build three routes to the goal. Each one must be different in one clear way: short and exposed, long and covered, or high and requiring a jump.

Build every route to the metrics of the character, which are the numbers for what it can do. Before you build, test in PIE how high a step the character can walk up, how high a ledge it can jump onto and how wide a gap it can jump over, and write the numbers down. Do not guess any step heights. If you have a metrics test level of your own, use the numbers from it.
Connect at least two of the routes somewhere in the middle, so that the player can switch from one to the other.
Start PIE and walk each route from the start to the goal. Fix anything that stops you.

LDQ14.brief: People find their way by what they can see. A sightline is a clear line of view from where the player stands to something in the distance. A landmark is a large object with a shape that is easy to recognize, which tells the player where they are and where to go. In this quest you add a landmark near the goal of a level, check where it can be seen from, and build a reveal, a moment where a hidden view opens up.
checklist: Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open a level of your own that has a start, a goal and more than one route between them. If you have none, block out a quick one in a new level: a start and a goal about 40 to 60 m apart, with two or three different routes made of cubes and walls between them. Add one landmark near the goal. It should be tall and have a unique silhouette (outline), for example a tower, a big arch or a dead tree.
Check that the landmark is visible from the start and from at least one point on every route. Check this in PIE at eye height, not with the flying editor camera.
Block one sightline on purpose with a wall. Then open the view again at a corner to make a reveal.
Save a bookmark at each point where the landmark first comes into view.

LDQ15.brief: Players follow light, color and shape more than they follow signs. You can use these three things as quiet hints that tell the player where to go and what they can use. In this quest you choose one guidance color, light the route entrances, add a shape hint, and check every junction in a level.
checklist: Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open a level of your own that has a start, a goal and more than one route between them. If you have none, block out a quick one in a new level: a start and a goal about 40 to 60 m apart, with two or three different routes made of cubes and walls, and at least one ledge to jump onto. Pick one guidance color, for example yellow = climbable or usable. Make a Material Instance for it, with a name that starts with MI_, and use it only for that meaning.
Apply it to every ledge the player can jump onto and to every usable object in the level. Nothing else gets that color.
Light the entrance of each route so that it is slightly brighter than the walls around it.
Give one route a shape cue, which is a shape that points the way: an arch, a gap in a wall, or a line of pillars that points toward the route.
Start PIE and stop at each junction. Ask yourself what tells you to go this way. Fix every junction where you have no answer.

LDQ16.brief: Verticality means using height in a level, with places above and below the main floor. Height adds new routes and good views, but only when the character can really climb it. In this quest you raise a route with a ramp, stairs and a ledge, and you size every piece from the measured limits of the character.
checklist: Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open BP_ThirdPersonCharacter, select Character Movement, and write down Max Step Height and Walkable Floor Angle. Test in PIE how high a ledge the character can jump onto. Then open a level of your own that has a route from a start to a goal, or block out a simple route of about 40 m in a new level. Raise the route by 3 to 4 m. Use a ramp, a staircase and one ledge that the player must jump up onto.
Make each stair riser (the height of one stair) lower than Max Step Height. Make the ramp less steep than Walkable Floor Angle.
Size the ledge and any gap with a margin. They should be noticeably below the maximum jump you measured, not right at it.
Add a way back down from the high point, such as a drop or stairs, so that it is not a trap.
Start PIE and climb every piece three times. If you miss even once, the piece is too close to the limit.

Pick a level that you built yourself, with a start, a goal and at least two routes. If you have none, block out a quick one first in a project made from the Third Person template: a start and a goal about 40 to 60 m apart, with two or three different routes between them. Before you go on, take a break of at least one hour away from the level.
Save review bookmarks with Ctrl+1 to Ctrl+5: one at the start, one at each route entrance, and one at the goal.
At each bookmark, press G to turn on Game View, which hides the editor icons, and take a screenshot.
Play the whole level once in PIE as if you had never seen it. Write a note every time you hesitate, look around or get lost.
Pick the two worst notes and fix those problems. Then take new screenshots from the same bookmarks.

quiz.q: How do you save and recall a camera bookmark?
choices: Ctrl+number to save, number to recall
quiz.explain: Hold Ctrl and press a number key to save the camera position, and press the number key alone to return to it. Bookmarks are saved with the level.

quiz.q: Why review from the same bookmarks every time?
choices: Before/after comparisons are only fair from the same camera
quiz.explain: Same view, same framing, so what you compare is the change.

quiz.q: What does G do in the level viewport?
choices: Toggles Game View, hiding editor icons and gizmos
quiz.explain: Game View shows roughly what the player would see, without editor clutter.

quiz.q: During a self-playtest, what should you write down?
choices: Every place you hesitate, backtrack or look around unsure
Nothing, just fix things as you go
quiz.explain: Hesitation is the signal. Note it first, fix it after. Fixing as you go hides patterns.

quiz.q: Why take a break before reviewing?
choices: You stop seeing problems in a space you just built. Time away brings back some fresh eyes
quiz.explain: It's the closest you get to a new player without asking one.

LDQ18.brief: The first job of lighting in a level is to show the player the route and the dangers. Looking pretty comes second. The Lighting Only view mode shows the level with light but without textures, so you can judge the brightness alone. In this quest you check the lighting of a level with several routes, make the goal the brightest point, and make sure an enemy would stand out against the background.
checklist: Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open a level of your own that has a start, a goal and more than one route. If you have none, block out a quick one in a new level: a start and a goal about 40 to 60 m apart, with two or three routes made of cubes and walls. Lock the exposure, so that the brightness does not change by itself: add a Post Process Volume, tick Infinite Extent (Unbound), and in its Exposure section set Metering Mode to Manual and adjust Exposure Compensation until you can see the level clearly.
Switch the viewport to the Lighting Only view mode. Check that each route entrance is brighter than the walls around it.
Light the goal area so that it is the brightest point in the level.
Place a mannequin where an enemy might stand. Adjust the lights until its silhouette (outline) is easy to see against the background.
Remove or dim any light that pulls attention toward a dead end.
Save two camera bookmarks with Ctrl+1 and Ctrl+2, for example at the start and at a route entrance. Switch back to Lit mode and check the level again from these bookmarks.

quiz.q: Why check readability in the Lighting Only view mode?
choices: It removes material color so you see only light and value contrast
quiz.explain: If the route reads without textures, it will read with them.

quiz.q: Which area should usually be the brightest?
choices: The goal or the next place you want the player to go
quiz.explain: Players move toward light. Put the brightest spot where you want them to go.

quiz.q: An enemy blends into a dark wall. Which fix helps most?
choices: Light the wall behind it or add rim light so its silhouette separates
quiz.explain: Combat readability comes from silhouette against background, not overall brightness.

quiz.q: Why keep exposure locked while doing this pass?
choices: Auto exposure would brighten dark routes and hide the problem
quiz.explain: Locked exposure shows the real brightness difference between routes. With auto exposure the picture adapts, and a route that is too dark looks fine after a moment.

quiz.q: Six colored lights in one room, none meaning anything. The issue?
choices: Visual noise that competes with your guidance cues
quiz.explain: If you use color to guide the player, light color should support that rule and not compete with it.

LDQ20.brief: A courtyard is an open space with walls around it, and it is a good size for a first complete level. This quest lets you combine several level design skills in one piece of work: metrics, routes, a landmark, guidance and readable lighting. You build one small courtyard with three routes to a goal, review it, and send screenshots, a map and a short writeup. Everything you need to build is listed in the steps.
checklist: Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Test in PIE how high a step the character can walk up, how high a ledge it can jump onto and how wide a gap it can jump over, and write these metrics down. Create a new level named L_Courtyard. Build an enclosed courtyard with one entrance and one goal, and build everything to your metrics.

Build three routes to the goal that differ in a clear way, such as length, risk, height or cover. At least one route must use height, with a ramp, stairs or a ledge, and at least two routes must connect.

Add one landmark, a tall object with an outline that is easy to recognize, that is visible from the entrance and from each route. Choose one guidance color for things the player can climb or use, and use it only for that.

Do a lighting pass for readability. First lock the exposure: add a Post Process Volume, tick Infinite Extent (Unbound), and set Metering Mode to Manual in its Exposure section. Then light the level so that the goal is the brightest point and the dead ends are dim. Check it in the Lighting Only view mode.
Save 3 review bookmarks with Ctrl+1 to Ctrl+3: one at the entrance, one at a point in the middle of a route, and one at the goal. Take a screenshot of each in Game View (press G).
Take a top-down screenshot in the orthographic Top view, which shows the level from above without perspective. Draw the three routes on it in different colors.
Take a break of at least one hour. Then play the level once yourself as if you had never seen it, note where you hesitate, and fix the worst problem you find.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT part of the capstone turn-in?
quiz.explain: Packaging comes much later. Rank 1 is screenshots, map and writeup.

quiz.q: How do you get a clean top-down map of the courtyard?
choices: Switch the viewport to Top (orthographic) and screenshot it
quiz.explain: Orthographic Top has no perspective distortion, so routes and sizes read true.

quiz.q: What makes the three routes count as three?
choices: They differ in a clear way, like length, risk, height or cover
quiz.explain: A route only counts if choosing it changes something for the player.

quiz.q: The goal is hard to find in the Lighting Only view. What do you redo?
choices: The names of the Material Instances
quiz.explain: The goal should be the brightest point. Fix the lighting before adding detail.

quiz.q: Which bookmarks does the capstone ask for?
choices: Entrance, a mid-route point, and the goal
quiz.explain: Three fixed views let a reviewer judge the space the way you did.

checklist: Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one, and open the template map. If you prefer, block out a quick courtyard in a new level with a floor, walls and 2 exits.
Start PIE and walk through the space. Write 3 notes: where you hesitated, what drew your eye, and one place where the space felt too tight or too big.
For each note, press F8 to eject, which lets you leave the character and fly the camera freely while the game runs. Take a screenshot of the spot.

quiz.q: What's the most useful thing to note while walking a level?
choices: Where you hesitated or got lost
quiz.explain: Hesitation shows where the space failed to guide you.

quiz.q: What does F8 do in PIE?
choices: Ejects from the pawn so you can fly around the running game
quiz.explain: Eject lets you leave the character while the game keeps running, so that you can frame the problem spot for your screenshot.

quiz.q: A doorway feels too tight. What's it usually measured against?
choices: The camera's field of view only
The character capsule plus comfort margin
quiz.explain: Level designers size spaces from character metrics, such as the width of the capsule and how high the character can jump.

LDQ1.brief: The Water plugin gives Unreal ready-made lakes, rivers and oceans that you can place in a level. In level design, water is a useful edge: it shows the player where the route ends without a wall. In this quest you add a lake or a river to a terrain and let a path run beside it.
checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Open Edit > Plugins, search for Water, enable the Water plugin and restart the editor.

Open a level of your own that has a Landscape with a path on it. If you have none, create a new level, open Landscape Mode, choose New on the Manage tab, and sculpt a simple path across the terrain. Open the Place Actors panel (Window > Place Actors), search for Water Body, and drag a Water Body Lake or a Water Body River into the level. A water body is shaped by a spline, a line with points you can move: select the water, then click and move its points to change the outline.
Use the water as a boundary that the path runs beside. It should not be a blocker that the player cannot understand.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Open a level of your own that has a goal, a landmark and at least one dead end. If you have none, block out a quick one in a new Basic level: two or three routes of cubes and walls from a start to a goal, a tall landmark near the goal, and one side path that ends at a wall. Save a camera bookmark with Ctrl+1 and take a screenshot for the before picture. Select the Exponential Height Fog actor in the Outliner. If the level has none, drag one in from the Place Actors panel, under Visual Effects. In the Details panel, turn on Volumetric Fog.

In the Place Actors panel, search for Local Fog Volume and drag one over one dead end. Scale it so that it covers the dead end, and raise its two Extinction values in the Details panel, which make the fog thicker, until the dead end feels less inviting.
Check that you can still see the goal and the landmark clearly through the fog.

Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on, and open any level with a floor and at least one doorway or route entrance. Open the Place Actors panel, search for Decal, and drag a Decal Actor onto a floor or wall. In its Details panel, set Decal Material to a decal material. If your project has none, make a simple one: create a material, set its Material Domain to Deferred Decal and its Blend Mode to Translucent, and connect a color and an opacity.

Use 3 to 4 decals, such as scuffs, arrows or stains, to lead toward one route entrance. Hold Alt and drag a decal to copy it. A decal only shows where its box touches a surface, so rotate and move each one until you see it.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. In any level, build a small blockout room from cubes (a floor and four walls), or use a room you already have. Select all the actors of the room. Right-click the selection, open Level and choose Create Level Instance. Click OK in the window that opens and save the new level file, for example as L_Room_Instance.
Place the instance two more times in the level, so that you have three. Hold Alt and drag the instance to make a copy.

Select one copy and click Edit in the Details panel. Change something, for example move a wall. Then select the Level Instance in the Outliner and click Commit Changes in the Details panel. Confirm that the change shows up in all three copies.

LDQ5.brief: A landscape spline is a curved line that you draw on a landscape with control points. Unreal can then shape the ground to follow that line, which is a fast way to make roads and paths. In this quest you draw a spline up a hill and flatten the landscape under it so that the path is easy to walk.
checklist: Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open a level of your own that has a Landscape with a hill. If you have none, create a new level, open Landscape Mode, choose New on the Manage tab, and raise one hill with the Sculpt tool. In Landscape Mode, go to the Manage tab and select the Splines tool.
Hold Ctrl and click on the landscape to place control points from the low ground up to the top of the hill.

Deform the landscape to the spline, so that the path sits flat and is walkable: in the settings of the Splines tool, under Deform Landscape to Splines, click All Splines. If the path is too narrow, select the control points and raise their Width in the Details panel, then click the button again.

LDQ6.brief: PCG means Procedural Content Generation. It is a system in Unreal where you build a graph of rules, and the graph places many objects for you. To scatter means to spread objects over an area. In this quest you take a first look at PCG: you scatter one rock mesh inside a volume and keep it away from a path.
checklist: Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Open a level of your own that has a Landscape, or create a new level, open Landscape Mode and choose New on the Manage tab. Decide where a path runs across it. Open Edit > Plugins, enable the Procedural Content Generation Framework (PCG) plugin and restart the editor. Right-click in the Content Browser, open PCG and choose PCG Graph. The graph holds the rules. Then drag a PCG Volume from the Place Actors panel onto the landscape, and set Graph on its PCG component in the Details panel. The volume is the box that marks where the graph works.

Open the graph. Add a Get Landscape Data node, a Surface Sampler node and a Static Mesh Spawner node, and connect them in that order. In the Static Mesh Spawner, add one entry under Mesh Entries and pick one rock mesh, for example the rock in the Props folder of the Starter Content. Select the PCG Volume and click Generate in the Details panel. The rocks appear on the landscape inside the volume.
Move the volume away from the path, so that the scattered rocks do not block it.

LDQ7.brief: A level that is easy to read in daylight can become confusing at night. The same rules still apply: the player must be able to see the route entrances and the goal. In this quest you make a night copy of a level with several routes and use local lights, such as Point Lights and Spot Lights, to keep it readable.
checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Open a daylight level of your own that has a start, a goal and more than one route. If you have none, block out a quick one in a new Basic level: a start and a goal about 40 to 60 m apart, with two or three routes made of cubes and walls. Save 3 camera bookmarks with Ctrl+1 to Ctrl+3 and take a screenshot from each. Then duplicate the level in the Content Browser and add _Night to the name of the copy, for example L_Routes_01_Night.

In the copy, select the Directional Light, which is the sun. Rotate it until it sits low over the horizon, lower its Intensity until the level is dim, and set its Light Color to a cool blue so that it reads as moonlight. Lock the exposure so that the picture does not brighten by itself: add a Post Process Volume, tick Infinite Extent (Unbound), and set Metering Mode to Manual in its Exposure section.
Add local lights so that every route entrance and the goal are still easy to see.

LDQ8.brief: Sound can guide a player just like light can. A sound that gets louder as you get closer pulls the player toward its source. Attenuation is the setting that controls how a sound gets quieter with distance, and reverb is the echo of a room. In this quest you place a looping sound near the goal of a level, set how far it reaches, and change the reverb of one room.
checklist: Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Open a level of your own that has a goal and at least one room. If you have none, block out a quick one in a new level: a start, a goal about 40 m away, and one closed room on the way. Drag a looping sound from the Content Browser into the level, near the goal. This creates an Ambient Sound actor. The Starter Content has looping sounds in its Audio folder that you can use.

Select the Ambient Sound actor. In the Details panel, under Attenuation, turn on Override Attenuation. Set Inner Radius and Falloff Distance so that the player can hear the sound from the start, and so that it is louder near the goal.

In the Place Actors panel, open Volumes and drag an Audio Volume around one room. In its Details panel, under Reverb, turn on Apply Reverb and pick a Reverb Effect. Walk into the room in PIE and listen to the change.

LDQ9.brief: A Landscape Grass Type is an asset that lets the landscape material place grass by itself, on the layers you choose. The Grass Quick Start is the page in the Unreal documentation that shows how to set this up. In this quest you follow that guide on a terrain and keep a path free of grass.
checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Open a level of your own that has a Landscape, or create a new level, open Landscape Mode and choose New on the Manage tab. Follow the Grass Quick Start guide that is linked on this quest on that landscape. It has you create one Landscape Grass Type asset, add a grass mesh to it, and connect it in the Landscape Material with a Landscape Grass Output node.

Paint a path layer that has no grass, so that the route stays clear. The grass only grows where its own layer is painted, so painting another layer, such as dirt, along the route removes the grass there.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template, and work in any level with open sky. Switch the editor to Modeling Mode with the mode dropdown in the main toolbar. If Modeling is not in the list, enable the Modeling Tools Editor Mode plugin in Edit > Plugins. Block out 3 landmark options with the shape tools, such as Box and Cylinder, and make them about the same height.
Look at each one from a distance against the sky. Open the view mode menu of the viewport, which shows Lit by default, and choose Unlit or Lighting Only, so that you judge only the shape.
Keep the one that you recognize the fastest, and note why.
